analysis.one_liner: Bars health insurers from denying coverage because a patient joined an approved clinical trial.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote: it sat in the Senate labor committee until Congress ended, with one sponsor and no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped health plans from denying, limiting, or adding conditions to coverage of care that a patient receives as part of an approved clinical study, such as a cancer or NIH research trial. Insurers could still refuse to pay for the research itself — the sponsor's bill only required them to cover the routine care the patient would have gotten anyway, when the only reason it was being denied was the patient's trial participation. The bill was referred to the Senate committee that handles health legislation and never went anywhere.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients with serious illnesses who want to join federally or independently approved clinical trials. Many insurers at the time treated trial-related care as experimental and excluded it, leaving patients to pay out of pocket or forgo trials that might offer their best treatment option.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients with serious illnesses seeking trial access

how_it_helps.text: Health plans could not deny, limit, or impose extra conditions on coverage of items and services a patient receives while in an approved clinical study, and could not discriminate against the enrollee for participating [S2][S3].

Coverage applies to care furnished according to the study's design or to treat problems resulting from participation, as long as the plan would have covered those services outside the trial context [S3].
The bill does not require plans to pay for the research itself — items normally paid for as part of the study stay on the study's budget, which narrows the cost to insurers [S3].

'Approved clinical study' covers trials cleared by HHS, NIH, FDA, VA, Defense, or a qualified nongovernmental research entity, so both government-sponsored and peer-reviewed private trials count [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers, which could no longer treat clinical trial participation as a reason to deny coverage of routine care, and the plans' other enrollees to the extent costs are passed into premiums.

drawbacks.text: The mandate applies to all health plans, including employer plans, so it adds a federal requirement on private benefit design; insurers would bear the cost of covering routine care during trials, some of which could flow into premiums [S3].

The bill does not require plans to pay the study's own costs, so patients and research sponsors could still face bills for the investigational parts of a trial — the protection covers routine care only [S3].
The definition of approved studies is broad, including qualified nongovernmental research entities, which insurers could argue invites disputes over which trials qualify [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A targeted patient protection: it extends coverage only to care a plan would already pay for outside a trial, so the added cost is limited, while the benefit for a patient facing a life-threatening illness — access to an experimental option without losing coverage — is large. The main design weakness is that it does nothing about the study's own costs, so out-of-pocket exposure for the research itself remains.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate committee that handles health bills, and that was the last thing that ever happened to it.

narrative.text: Senator Olympia Snowe introduced the bill on March 29, 1996, and delivered introductory remarks [S1][S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources, its only committee action [S5].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers kept the ability to exclude clinical trial care from coverage. Patients with serious illnesses who might have joined trials continued to face denial of coverage for trial-related routine care.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers kept their coverage exclusions

for.name: Olympia Snowe
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; it was her only action before the Congress ended

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action: no hearing, no markup, no vote; the bill died there when the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill had a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan pattern can be read from the record.

industries.note: The bill would have barred plans from using clinical trial participation as a reason to deny or condition coverage of routine care. Insurers' savings from treating trial care as experimental would have ended, and their gain under the status quo came directly at the expense of sick patients' access.

industries.industry: Medical research and clinical trial sponsors
industries.note: Easier insurance coverage of trial-related care makes patients more willing to enroll, which helps trials fill their slots and move research forward. The bill keeps research costs on study budgets rather than shifting them to insurers.
